title: Rashi on the Talmud
hook: Rashi explains word by word; without him most learners would be lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, the page, and your line: the page is a conversation. The center block, and the columns cupped around it. Today we sit down in the inner margin, next to the one who explains. Day one thousand one hundred.

A first-time learner is stuck on one Aramaic word. The line runs on with hardly a pause, and nothing says who is speaking. The page feels like a locked door. A teacher leans over and taps the narrow column at the inside of the page. Start there. Don't read it all. Just find the note on the word you're stuck on. You find it: a few words copied from the text, then a short, plain sentence. The door opens a crack. One word at a time. Today, who is sitting in that column.
screen: `A LOCKED DOOR.` → `START IN THE NARROW COLUMN.` → `ONE WORD AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Rashi on the Talmud. Rashi is the name formed from the initials of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, a teacher in medieval France, in the town of Troyes. He wrote commentary on the Torah and on the Talmud, and his Talmud commentary is the one printed in the inner margin. First, how it works. Each comment opens with a few words copied from the Gemara, a heading, so you can match it to the spot you're stuck on. Then comes a short explanation: what this word means, who is speaking, what the question is. He moves with the text, line by line, rarely stopping to argue. Second, what he does for an argument. Remember the first page of Berakhot, the evening Shema? Rashi pauses there on a practice of his own day: people recited the Shema in the synagogue before dark. So how does that fit the mishnah's time? He explains that the evening service is said to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, and that the main duty is fulfilled by the Shema said at bedtime. A short note, and suddenly the text touches a real evening. Third, his own language. Sometimes Rashi glosses a hard word with a word in the French of his day, written in Hebrew letters, so some scholars now read him for old French as well. Some learners say that without Rashi the Talmud would stay closed to them. He doesn't argue with the text. He walks beside you through it. The guide.
screen: `A TEACHER IN TROYES.` · `A HEADING, THEN A SHORT NOTE.` · `THE SHEMA BEFORE DARK.` · `OLD FRENCH IN HEBREW LETTERS.` · then, large: `THE GUIDE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to read one Rashi comment, and you just heard one. Close your eyes, if that helps. Picture the narrow column at the inside of the page. A heading: from when. Then the note: people pray at the synagogue before dark, and the main duty is the Shema at bedtime. Let that land in your own evening. Where do you end your day? On the breath in, from when. On the breath out, at bedtime. Let one small, steady voice walk beside you for a while. The bell holds the time.
Rashi on the Talmud. The commentary in the inner margin that explains the Gemara word by word, heading by heading. Today's word.
Your line: the guide. Today, when you explain something to someone, try Rashi's way: find the exact word they're stuck on, explain only that, and let them keep walking. Day one thousand one hundred.

howItsDone: Talmud learners read Rashi's commentary alongside the Gemara, matching each comment's heading words to the line they are studying; in a class, the teacher often reads the Gemara and Rashi together, line by line.

fork.setup: people in your community recite the evening Shema in the synagogue while it's still light. the mishnah's time hasn't come yet. you're Rashi, writing your note. what do you explain?
options: that the synagogue practice is simply wrong.
that the service stands prayer on words of Torah, and the main duty is the Shema at bedtime.
that the time in the mishnah doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: Rashi explains the early recital as a way to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, with the main duty fulfilled by the bedtime Shema. a short note that touches a real evening.

original.note: Hebrew: Rashi, from the initials of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rashi is a footnote for beginners.
what it means: the running guide in the inner margin, explaining the Gemara heading by heading.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Berakhot 2a on the evening Shema and the bedtime Shema, his old French glosses in Hebrew letters, and the semi-cursive typeface later named Rashi script.

sources.ref: Rashi on Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 2a (s.v. me-eimatai)

notes: The hook is an illustrative scene of a first-time learner and a teacher, not a quoted person.
Rashi on Berakhot 2a is paraphrased: the synagogue recital before dark is to 'stand in prayer from words of Torah', and the main obligation is the Shema at bedtime. Please confirm.
Biographical facts (the name from the initials of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki; Troyes; commentary on Torah and Talmud) are stated without a cited text; no dates are given, by design.
Rashi's old French glosses (la'azim) are mentioned in general; please confirm the phrasing.
The index hook says 'without him most learners would be lost'; the script softens this to 'learners say that without Rashi the Talmud would be closed to them', under the claims rule.
The trapdoor mentions 'Rashi script', the typeface named after him later; please confirm.
